facts.value: 26-page Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (excl. appendices) (doc 77176) taken to Full Council on 26 February 2026 as agenda item. Report author: Peter Worth, Interim Treasury Management Accountant. Contact block (para 15.1) names Terry Colllier [sic -- three L's, address uses correct T.Collier], S.151 Officer, T.Collier@spelthorne.gov.uk. Appendices A (MRP Policy), B (Annual Investment Strategy), C (Approved Counterparty List), D (Approved Countries), E (CIPFA TMC requirements) are excluded from this PDF but the treasury tables and prudential indicators are ALL in the main body -- no companion papers needed to reconcile. Read in full from local PDF. Council is under Statutory Direction issued 8 May 2025 (para 3.10) and is due to be abolished on 31 March 2027 under Surrey local government reorganisation, with 'West Surrey' as the successor authority (para 4.67).

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (excl appendices) -- Council, 26 February 2026

facts.note: Officer address is in the paper itself (para 15.1) -- unusual for a strategy paper. Take verbatim. The name is printed as 'Terry Colllier' with three L's -- almost certainly a typo since the email address uses 'T.Collier'. Use 'Terry Collier' in the salutation.

facts.value: TIES within rounding. Our PWLB file for SPELTHORNE BOROUGH COUNCIL (price_book.py --as-at 2026-03-31): 118 loans / £712,284,441 principal / weighted 4.6232% / mix 117 MATURITY + 1 ANNUITY. Paper Table 6 (p.12), 2025/26 Forecast Gross Projected debt: £713m -- ties to £0.7m (0.1%). Paper para 4.41 (p.15), post-restructure balance sheet: £715m -- ties to £2.7m (0.4%). No post-restructure weighted rate is published in the paper against which to cross-check our 4.6232% (the 2.4% in para 4.39 is the pre-restructure rate at 31/3/25 on £1,057m of pre-2016 borrowing).

source.title: OUR file (price_book.py --as-at 2026-03-31); paper Table 6 and para 4.41

facts.note: Reconciliation ties. Additionally the MATURITY PROFILE of our file matches the paper's Chart 3 shape exactly. 20 loans of £138.6m under 12 months = the £140m July 2027 lump in Chart 3's 2027/28 bar (individual loans 880954-880973 at 4.53%). 50 loans of £494.4m in 5-10y bucket = the £275m July 2035 lump plus £161m July 2036 lump in Chart 3's 2035/36 and 2036/37 bars (loans 880979-881013 at 5.38%/5.47%). These are all November 2025 restructure loans -- round-number tranches, July 2027/2035/2036 maturity dates -- and they show up in our file with the shape the chart describes.

facts.value: TIES to the pound across all six years of Table 6. CFR - Gross Projected debt = Under/(over) borrowing. 24-25A 1170-1072=98 (Table 6 prints 98); 25-26F 1088-713=375 (prints 375); 26-27E 880-699=181 (prints 181); 27-28E 795-560=235 (prints 235); 28-29E 693-532=161 (prints 161); 29-30E 662-518=144 (prints 144). All six years tie exactly.
facts.note: Other Long-Term Liabilities (£2m in 24-25A, £1m in 25-26F, £0 from 26-27 onwards per Table 11) are absorbed into the paper's Gross Projected debt figures -- the identity closes with two terms not three because the paper netted OLL into the debt series.

facts.value: Paragraph 2.4 and 4.41: £905m of loans (all >10y remaining) restructured in November 2025, capturing a £342m (32%) discount and reducing the Balance Sheet debt from £1,057m at 31/3/25 to £715m post-restructure. Pre-restructure book was at 2.4% weighted average rate against a materially higher current PWLB environment. Our file's post-restructure weighted rate is 4.6232% -- consistent with new loans drawn at then-current PWLB rates in November 2025 (the 22 tranche parcels at 4.53% July-2027, 5.38% July-2035 and 5.47% July-2036 are all in our file). Of the seventy-plus councils read this year for the outreach programme, this is by a very wide margin the largest single restructure event observed. Nearest comparators in the library: Warwickshire £4.5m early repayment saving; Tameside £2.8m break discount captured. £342m is two orders of magnitude larger.

source.title: Paras 2.4, 4.39-4.41; price_book.py output for SPELTHORNE BOROUGH COUNCIL

facts.value: Our engine (DMO premature repayment curve, notice 314/26 PM 2026-08-14) prices 114 live loans: balance £707,557,866; indicative settlement £716,688,039; net PREMIUM £9,130,174 (1.3% of principal). 86 loans below par, 28 above. Largest premiums are on the £50m 5.38% July-2035 tranches (+£2.2m each) and £50m 5.47% July-2036 tranches (+£2.3m each). Largest discounts are on residual pre-restructure loans at 1.99-2.48% maturing 2032-2034 that survived the November restructure (small residual balances, maximum discount -£1.07m on PW505398 at 2.09%).
facts.note: The book has largely repriced above par at today's DMO curve. INDICATIVE ONLY -- only the DMO can quote. Para 4.44 is explicit no further restructuring is planned before the demise; this figure is offered as context on what remains, not as a case for further action.

facts.value: Table 7 Ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream (PI 4a): 24-25A 254%; 25-26F 309%; 26-27E 319%; 27-28E 231%; 28-29E 206%; 29-30E 173%. Para 4.31 states 'the ratio of capital financing charges to the net revenue stream at 31 March 2030 remains high at 169%. Many comparator authorities are currently reporting a ratio of 18% or less.' (Table 7 prints 173% for 29-30 -- para 4.31 says '169%'. Minor internal inconsistency; both make the same qualitative point.) Table 8 including net income from investment property: 74/91/85/71/71/73%. Table 9 IP income share of NRS: 243/238/275/226/191/138%.
facts.note: The 319% peak in 2026/27 is on the paper's own printed numbers against a 18% peer comparator the paper itself cites -- so quoting both back is quoting the paper. Not a comparison of our making.

facts.value: Council abolished 31 March 2027 (para 4.67) -- successor authority is 'West Surrey' under Surrey local government reorganisation. Successor inherits from Table 6: £699m gross debt at 26-27 forecast year-end, reducing through the CFR/MRP mechanism to £518m by 29-30 estimate. Maturity concentration (Chart 3, matched to our file): £140m in FY 2027/28 (July 2027 lump), £275m in 2035/36 (July 2035), £161m in 2036/37 (July 2036). Para 4.48 explicitly notes that the £161m 2036/37 balance 'has been left to mature in 2036/37 so that the successor authority has flexibility to re-finance or redeem the borrowing; or re-visit the current Council's current asset rationalisation plan'. Loans to subsidiaries £44.8m at 31/3/25 (Table 4) -- Knowle Green Estates £44.6m at rates below Council's pre-restructure borrowing rate ('no margin added to allow for credit risk or a return', para 4.63), Spelthorne Direct Services £249k at 5%. Para 4.67 confirms 'the terms of any future loans to third parties will be the responsibility of the successor authority (West Surrey)'.
facts.note: The paper is explicitly a handover document. Tone the email accordingly -- there is no future policy iteration at Spelthorne to influence, and the S151 (Terry Collier) is likely handling the abolition/handover. The value we offer is (i) the reconciliation, (ii) the sector-level context on the scale of the £342m restructure, (iii) what remains for West Surrey to pick up.

facts.value: Para 4.11: 'a substantial investment property portfolio valued at £552m (at 31 March 2025)'. Chart 1 (p.11) shows portfolio peaked ~£995m in 2018/19-2019/20; ~£583m at 31/3/25 axis reading (£552m in the para text -- minor inconsistency of the same figure between chart and text). Para 4.15: 'the Council is at risk of realising losses of £442m from disposing of the investment portfolio at current values.' Table 3 performance indicators at 31/3/25: debt-to-net-service-expenditure 3,443% (benchmark <25%); loan-to-value ratio 164% (benchmark <80%); investment cover ratio 1.19 (benchmark >3); benchmark returns -14.7% (benchmark 5.0%). Para 4.13: gross rental income £44.5m 2024/25 / net General Fund contribution £39.6m after direct operating costs. Table 8 shows the ratio of financing costs INCLUDING net IP income is 74-91% -- still high but materially below the 254-319% headline; para 4.32 acknowledges this remains 'well above the ratio reported by most comparable authorities'.
facts.note: The IP portfolio is not treasury debt but it is what the debt-reduction strategy rests on -- Table 5 requires £293m of capital receipts by 2029/30 to bring CFR from £1,088m to £662m, of which £155m needs to come in 2026/27 alone. Delivering that from an IP book that is 43% below cost with a loan-to-value of 164% is the execution risk. Not for email -- this is macro context beyond what the treasury paper itself is asking of the reader.

facts.value: Para 4.52: as at 15 December 2025 cash balances and short-term investments totalled £37.2m, of which £30m invested with other local authorities for periods not exceeding 12 months. Para 4.53: forecast average balance £13.5m during 2026/27. Para 4.55: BoE cut base rate on 18 December 2025 to 3.75%, expected 3.25-3.5% by mid-late 2026; MMFs forecast 3.75%. Para 4.56: 'Inter-local authority lending continues provide returns of around 4.20%.' Para 4.61: strategy is to continue lending surplus money out to other LAs 'as these currently provide the best short-term returns with good security'. Table 13: upper limit for principal sums invested more than 364 days = £70m across all years (£44.8m subsidiaries + potential extended LA loans).
facts.note: Spelthorne is on the LENDER side of the LA-to-LA market at £30m -- similar shape to Rushmoor (£27m lent) and other net-investor districts read this year. Not the strongest observation for this paper's hook (the £342m restructure is the story) but worth recording for cross-council pattern-tracking.

facts.value: Table 14 (Summary of Prudential Indicators, p.21) carries multiple internal inconsistencies with the source Tables 5-9: (i) PI 2 CFR shows 796/694 for 27-28/28-29 vs Table 5 shows 795/693 (£1m rounding); (ii) PI 3 Under/(over) borrowed 99/376/181/236/162 vs Table 6 shows 98/375/181/235/161 (£1m rounding); (iii) PI 4a 254/309/319/206/166 vs Table 7 shows 254/309/319/231/206/173 -- Table 14 values for 27-28 and 28-29 do not match and appear either shifted a year or drawn from an earlier draft; (iv) PI 4b 74/91/85/63/57 vs Table 8 shows 74/91/85/71/71/73 -- materially different in 27-28 (63 vs 71) and 28-29 (57 vs 71); (v) PI 5a Auth limit 1170/1088/880/796/694 vs Table 11 shows 1170/1088/880/795/693. Also para 4.46 refers to 'Table 4' for the CFR which is actually in Table 5 (Table 4 is Company Investments). Table 12 (maturity limits) shows 0% upper limit on 21-30y, 31-40y, 41-50y buckets that carry 25%, 29%, 11% actual maturity respectively -- either the column is mis-labelled or the limits are set below actual position (inconsistent with Table 14 row 7 which shows only two enforceable limits: upper 5% under 12 months, lower 10% over 10 years). Table 10 (target asset sales) shows figures 23/155/48/67/0/252 with header '£000s' and Total 544 -- given para 4.25 refers to £293m of capital receipts and Table 5 shows £155m capital receipts applied in 2026/27, the values are clearly £m not £000s.

signals.headline: £905m of PWLB restructured November 2025 capturing £342m (32%) discount -- CFR falls from £1,170m (24-25A) to £662m (29-30E); external debt from £1,072m to £518m over the same window (Tables 5, 6)
signals.why_it_matters: Largest single restructure event observed in the seventy-plus councils read this year. Executed under Statutory Direction (8 May 2025) that required a strict debt-reduction plan; the resulting new PWLB book (£712m in our file, 4.62% weighted) is the shape the successor authority West Surrey inherits when Spelthorne is abolished on 31 March 2027.

signals.headline: Post-restructure maturity is heavily bunched: £140m matures July 2027 (successor's first year), £275m July 2035, £161m July 2036 -- the last of which para 4.48 explicitly leaves for the successor authority to decide about
signals.why_it_matters: The successor unitary (West Surrey) inherits both the debt and its refinancing decisions. The July 2027 lump falls in the successor's opening months; the 2035/36 concentration is 61% of the current £712m book falling due in two consecutive years. Not a signal about Spelthorne's own future policy -- there isn't one -- but a signal about what any successor authority receives on day one.

signals.headline: Table 3 property performance indicators at 31/3/25: debt-to-net-service-expenditure 3,443% (benchmark <25%); loan-to-value 164% (<80%); investment cover 1.19 (>3); benchmark returns -14.7% (5.0%). Prudential Indicator 4a financing/revenue ratio 319% at 26-27 peak against a comparator of 18% or less (para 4.31)
signals.why_it_matters: Every property performance benchmark is breached by a large multiple. Financing/revenue at 4a is 17x the comparator. Paper cites the sub-18% comparator itself so this is quoting the council's own figures back, not a comparison of our making. This is what the Statutory Direction is addressing.

officer.body:
Hi Terry,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has moved since. So below are a few thoughts on Spelthorne's 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 26 February. You're not being singled out -- every authority gets one of these -- and there's no agenda in it. The paper is candid about the position it inherited and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The starting cross-check first, which is where we start on any paper. Our PWLB file for Spelthorne holds 118 loans totalling £712,284,441 at a principal-weighted 4.6232%, against your Table 6 gross projected debt of £713m at the 2025/26 forecast year-end and the £715m post-restructure figure in paragraph 4.41. That ties within a rounding step. The maturity profile ties too -- your Chart 3 shows the £140m July 2027 lump, the £275m in July 2035 and the £161m in July 2036, and we hold each of those in the file as parcels drawn in November 2025 at 4.53%, 5.38% and 5.47% respectively. Your balance-sheet identity closes as well: CFR less gross projected debt reproduces the under-borrowing column of Table 6 to the pound in each of the six years.

What we don't have a benchmark for is the £342m of discount your paragraph 4.41 records against the £905m of loans restructured in November. Of the seventy-plus councils we've read this year, that is by a wide margin the largest single restructure event we've seen. The next largest we've priced in the library are Warwickshire's £4.5m in premature-repayment savings and Tameside's £2.8m break discount on an active portfolio manoeuvre; £342m is two orders of magnitude bigger, and it is what makes this paper unusual to read. Our monthly sector view at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity places what any given council drew alongside what everyone else did the same month, which is the sort of context most treasury papers don't carry.

What November built is what the successor authority inherits, and our loan-by-loan pricing engine puts an indicative net premium of about £9m across the live £708m balance today -- 86 loans below par, 28 above, priced against the DMO premature-repayment curve. The big 2035/36 and 2036/37 tranches are all showing above par at today's rates; the residual pre-restructure loans at 1.99-2.48% still sit below. That's indicative only -- only the DMO can quote a settlement -- and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled. Your paragraph 4.44 is explicit that no further restructuring is planned before the demise, so this is offered as context on what remains, not as a case for anything.

The £699m of gross projected debt at your 2026/27 year-end (Table 6) passes to West Surrey when it stands up. Your Table 7 financing-cost-to-revenue ratio is where the shape of the book shows up in the successor's revenue base -- 319% in 2026/27, still 173% at 2029/30 against the 18%-or-less comparator you cite in paragraph 4.31. Our liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is interactive and built on live data, which may be useful during the transition given that CIPFA has updates to both the Prudential and Treasury Codes coming.

On training, four fit the shape of this paper. PWLB & long-term borrowing strategy speaks to the November restructure and what the sector has been doing since; Debt restructuring & premature repayment covers the DMO curve mechanics we use to price break costs; Prudential Code refresh is timely given the code updates; and Reading treasury reports (for members) is written for the committees these go to.
